newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fears over Japan economy fade, but some wonder why.
newsitem.headline: Fears over Japan economy fade, but some wonder why.

text.p: Investors' fears that fiscal tightening would derail Japan's recovery are fading and some economists say the emerging optimism is overdue.
Others, however, warn the change of mood may prove as groundless as the deep gloom which gripped Tokyo's financial markets earlier this year.

Japanese authorities have argued for months that the pessimism which slashed Tokyo share prices and boosted bonds from the start of the year was overdone -- a sort of "irrational negative exuberance", to quote a well-known market mover, senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara.

Now a growing number of market players seem willing to give the official line some credence, a change of heart which helped boost Tokyo share prices more than three percent on Tuesday, in turn sparking a sharp fall in government bond futures.
Share prices were down moderately on Wednesday afternoon due to fears of overheating, but government bonds fell again.
"Until now a recession has been priced into the (bond) market but...no one's looking for a crash-and-burn scenario any more," said Andrew Shipley, economist at Schroders Japan.
A recent Merrill Lynch-Gallup poll of Japanese fund managers, for example, uncovered greater optimism among those surveyed about Japan's economic outlook.
"The idea that Japan would never grow faster than one percent is starting to be re-evaluated," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo.

Economists also pointed to a survey of 21 forecasters by London-based Consensus Economics Inc, which showed a mean April forecast for Japanese growth in calender 1997 of 1.6 percent, up from an earlier prediction of 1.4 percent. "The noteworthy thing was that the people forecasting total gloom and doom have disappeared," said Richard Jerram at ING Baring Securities.
The boost to exports from the weak yen, which has fallen around eight percent against the dollar since January, has been a plus for overall growth on which everyone agrees.
But with little hard data on hand, economists still differ over how robust domestic demand will be given higher taxes and lower public spending this current business year from April 1.

"On the whole, whatever data is available for the second quarter on consumer spending is not as negative as people thought, but there is not a lot of hard data to point to yet," said Peter Morgan, senior economist at HSCB James Capel.
Bulls argue that personal consumption and corporate capital spending can fuel the recovery this fiscal year rather than the heavy reliance on exports against which Washington has warned.
"The fact is, the recovery is being driven by domestic demand, rather than exports," said Schroders' Shipley.
Others see it differently.

"There is clearly a wind of optimism about the economy. Partly, it's a lot of happy talk about how much the problems in the financial sector are actually being solved," said Robert Feldman, chief economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
"I think they're dreaming," Feldman said. "We see essentially near-recession conditions for domestic demand."
Some near-term optimists, meanwhile, have nagging worries of their own, given that the recovery may even now be sowing the seeds of its destruction.
A further weakening of the yen and upward pressure on prices could set the stage for an earlier-than expected rise in Japan's rock-bottom interest rates, Schroders' Shipley said.
"Interest rates are poised to rise and if they rise too quickly, it could crush spending among service-sector firms."
